analysis.one_liner: Caps jury awards in medical malpractice lawsuits and shields doctors from suits over FDA-approved drugs.
analysis.headline: The bill never advanced past its committee referral; it died in the Senate with only two cosponsors and no vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The MCAP Act would rewrite the rules for medical malpractice lawsuits nationwide. It would cap compensation for pain and suffering at $250,000 per doctor or hospital (no more than $500,000 from multiple hospitals), sharply restrict punitive damages, limit lawyers' contingency fees, shorten deadlines for filing suit, and bar lawsuits naming a doctor who prescribed an FDA-approved drug or device. Economic losses like medical bills and lost wages would stay uncapped.
analysis.who_benefits: Doctors, hospitals, and medical malpractice insurers gain the most: caps and lawsuit restrictions lower their liability exposure and insurance payouts. Drug and device makers benefit indirectly, since prescribers could no longer be dragged into product liability suits over FDA-approved products.

how_it_helps.text: Caps noneconomic damages (pain and suffering) at $250,000 from any single provider or institution, and no more than $500,000 total from multiple institutions, while leaving economic damages like medical bills and lost earnings uncapped.

Makes punitive damages available only for malicious intent proven by clear and convincing evidence, caps them at the greater of two times economic damages or $250,000, and forbids juries from being told about the cap.
Bars health care providers from being named in product liability or class action lawsuits for prescribing or dispensing an FDA-approved drug, biological product, or device for an approved indication.
Limits attorneys' contingency fees on a sliding scale from 40% of the first $50,000 recovered down to 15% of anything above $600,000, and shortens the time injured patients have to file suit.

analysis.who_pays: Patients injured by medical negligence, especially those with catastrophic injuries whose lifetime suffering makes capped pain-and-suffering awards the core of their claim. State courts and juries would also lose their ability to set damages under state law.
analysis.who_pays_short: Patients seriously injured by medical negligence

drawbacks.text: The $250,000 cap on pain-and-suffering damages applies to the worst cases equally with minor ones; a child facing a lifetime of disability from a preventable birth injury would recover no more for that suffering than a patient with a far smaller injury.

The bill preempts state law wherever state rules give patients more room — longer filing deadlines, higher damages, or contingency fee arrangements — overriding states that chose stronger patient protections.

The bill would let courts reduce an award by health insurance or other benefits the patient already received, meaning an injured patient could see a jury's award shrink because their own coverage paid the bills.

Supporters' premise that lawsuit restrictions would meaningfully lower health care costs rests on the claim that malpractice litigation and defensive medicine drive up spending; the bill itself contains no provision guaranteeing that any savings reach patients through lower prices or premiums.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The gains would flow to the health care industry through lower liability exposure, while the costs would fall on a small group of the most seriously injured patients. There is an honest case for the bill — unpredictable jury awards and defensive medicine are real concerns, and economic damages remain uncapped — but the design spreads its benefit broadly across providers and insurers while concentrating its harm on exactly the patients with the largest, most life-altering injuries. It also overrides state law choices rather than letting states set their own balance.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee, which never took it up, and it died when the Congress ended in January 2015.

narrative.text: Sen. Rob Portman introduced the Medical Care Access Protection Act on January 22, 2013, joined by Sen. James Inhofe.
The bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions.
No further action was ever recorded — no hearings, no markup, no floor vote — through the end of the 113th Congress on January 3, 2015.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Injured patients and the plaintiffs' bar are better off because the bill died: state-law malpractice rights, uncapped jury awards, and existing filing deadlines remained in place. Providers, malpractice insurers, and drug and device makers never got the liability caps they sought.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Injured patients, who kept full malpractice rights

industries.note: Damage caps, shorter filing deadlines, and punitive-damage restrictions directly reduce what insurers must pay on claims. Their savings come out of the awards injured patients would otherwise receive.

The bill caps their malpractice exposure at $250,000 for pain-and-suffering awards and applies a fair-share rule limiting each defendant to its own share of blame. The relief to their bottom line is the cap on what injured patients can collect.

industries.industry: Prescription drug and medical device makers
industries.note: By barring suits against providers who prescribed FDA-approved products, the bill removes a litigation route that reaches manufacturers through prescribers, reducing legal pressure over drug and device safety.
Sliding-scale fee caps and lower recoveries cut both the awards they can win for clients and their own fees. Their interest in this bill ran with their injured clients'.
